newsitem.title: USA: Data show US economy ended second quarter at faster clip.
newsitem.headline: Data show US economy ended second quarter at faster clip.

text.p: U.S. economic activity quickened in June as orders for durable goods surged and sales of previously owned homes remained brisk, economic reports showed on Friday.

Orders for big-ticket items such as cars and appliances surpassed most economists' forecasts, while a separate report on sales of existing homes showed the housing market off slightly but still near its recent strong levels.
June durable goods orders jumped 2.3 percent, the largest increase since a 3.4 percent gain in January. Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast a 1.4 percent rise.
"The first half of the year ended on an upbeat note, setting the stage for a strong second half for the nation's manufacturing sector," said Ken Mayland, chief economist at KeyCorp in Cleveland.

Many experts had underestimated orders for transportation-related equipment, which usually account for about 20 percent of total durable goods orders. These orders surged 7.5 percent last month and comprised more than 70 percent of new durables ordered in June.

While the transportation segment could largely be dismissed as a fluke, other portions of the report showed gains that may have a longer-term impact. Non-defence capital goods orders, a forward-looking measure of companies' expansion plans, were particularly impressive in June.
Orders for capital goods, excluding defence-related equipment, jumped 5.4 percent in June. That compared with a 1.1 percent gain in May and a 1.7 percent decline in April.
Capital goods include machinery and other equipment that manufacturers use to boost capacity and increase efficiency.

"Typically, the equipment being purchased is electronic. It allows a factory to produce more and higher-quality goods more efficiently," said Kurt Karl, director of Wefa Group's U.S. forecasting centre in Pennsylvania.
Increased capital spending should pave the way for faster economic growth in the months ahead, but it will be "healthy" growth, Karl said.

The National Association of Realtors' existing home sales report offered somewhat mixed signals. Purchases of existing homes fell 2.6 percent to an annual rate of 4.14 million units as both housing prices and mortgage interest rates picked up.
Wall Street economists had projected a somewhat smaller decline, but a coinciding drop in home inventories suggested the housing market remains firm.
"Today's report is just a minor blip," said John Park, an economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co. "We should definitely start seeing the housing sector pick up steam in the third quarter."
The supply of homes on the market dipped to six months' worth in June from May's 6.8 months, indicating strong demand, the National Association of Realtors report showed.

The inventory levels were somewhat favourable, said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisers of Columbus, Ohio. Chan noted that any number below six months often is linked with heightened activity in the months ahead.
"Moving forward, we may fall below six months," Chan said, adding that the seasonally adjusted annual rate could climb above a 4.20 million-unit level.
In addition, long-term interest rates moved lower in July, which should provide stimulus for housing purchases and mortgage refinancings in the near term, Sanwa's Park said.

National Association of Realtors President Russell Booth said the underlying housing market should remain stable in the immediate future. "While there has been a slight tapering off, the market has remained strong due to favourable economic conditions," Booth said.

The financial markets digested both economic reports with little reaction. The 30-year bond's yield, which moves in the opposite direction of its price, rose to 6.46 percent from 6.44 percent at Thursday's close. The Dow Jones industrial average ended 3.49 points lower at 8,113.44.
